children: Stock futures are set to begin trading Sunday night after a roller coaster week fueled by unease over the artificial intelligence trade and future spending on AI data centers under the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress and Democratic-led state governments.

All three major stock indexes ended down last week, after Thursday's rout sent stock indexes on their biggest one-day percentage drop since April 4, 2025, which was the week after President Donald Trump announced his so-called "Liberation Day" global tariffs.
Fiduciary Capital Management said that "conditions for a broad equity bounce are not on the near-term horizon."

Whether Thursday was just a steeper step down in a broad rerating of AI prospects or a capitulation remains to be seen, "but given the sheer scale of money, debt, and future spending promises committed to the trade, we doubt that we will see any meaningful recovery in sentiment anytime soon," the analysts said.

They wrote in a Saturday note that AI skepticism has been present for months. "The Nasdaq essentially made all its 2026 gains in two months this year — April and May," they said, noting the index rose more than 27% in those months. But from June 1 to Nov. 1, the index was down 8.1%, they added.
"We've had a healthy market — just one overlaid with ongoing jitters about the tech trade," they said.

Although bonds have been a durable hedge against the tech wobbles, returning just over 2.6% from the beginning of October through this week, "that safe haven status seems like it is getting somewhat aged," they wrote. Markets see the Federal Reserve raising interest rates again in December. Economic growth that seems solid and inflation persistently well above target "is a recipe for further rate hikes as well."

Fiduciary Capital Management said it had previously believed that energy might be a durable hedge but "that thesis took a turn with the election results. The market's consensus now is that there will be a more urgent effort to end the Iran war."
Gasoline pump prices fell to an average of $4.020 a gallon on Sunday, down from $4.361 a gallon a month ago, but up from $3.073 a gallon a year ago, according to AAA.
Diesel prices declined to an average of $4.936 a gallon, from $5.270 a gallon a month ago, and $3.935 a gallon a year ago.
This week's economic highlights include the October consumer price index coming out Tuesday and the producer price index on Friday.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed down 0.9%, at 51,285.73, dropping 3.9% over its last two trading days, according to Dow Jones Market Data. The Dow is still up 6.7% this year.
The S&P 500 index closed down 2.7% at 7376.86, notching its largest one-week point and percentage decline since the week ending April 4, 2025. The S&P 500 is still up 7.8% year to date.
The Nasdaq Composite closed down 3.4% at 24,579.42, in its largest one-week point and percentage drop since the week ending Oct. 16. The Nasdaq is up 5.8% this year.
